questions.mappingNote: All fourteen parts directly assess graphical quadratic inequalities. Parts a–f already have factored quadratics; g–j require factorisation; k–n require rearrangement. Part n has exact irrational intercepts, found by square form before applying the same graphical sign method.
questions.methodNote: Example 2 rearranges the inequality to compare a quadratic with zero, identifies its x-intercepts, then selects where the parabola lies above, below or on the x-axis. Strict inequalities exclude intercepts; non-strict inequalities include them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find intercepts, interpret the sign of each parabola and distinguish included from excluded endpoints; the final part has irrational intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand both products, collect and factor the quadratic, then combine the two same-sign cases to obtain the exterior intervals.

questions.mappingNote: The main assessed task is a quadratic inequality; expansion and factorisation support the two-case sign analysis. Unlike question 4, this stem does not prescribe a graphical method.
questions.methodNote: The opening demonstration on page 15 solves a positive product by considering both factors positive or both negative. This applies after expansion and collection produce x(2x+13)>0.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand both products, collect terms and interpret the resulting quadratic inequality with a fractional boundary.

classification.difficultyReason: Find intercepts from supplied square forms, account for upward or downward opening, and translate the appropriate graph regions into inclusive or strict intervals.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess quadratic inequalities. Parts a, b, e, i and j use centred upward parabolas; c, d, g, k and l use translated upward parabolas; f and h use downward parabolas. Exact square roots retain the source's exact-answer convention.
questions.methodNote: Rearrange the inequality to compare a quadratic with zero, find its intercepts and read where its parabola is above, below or on the x-axis. Strict inequalities exclude intercepts; inclusive inequalities include them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use parabola signs and exact intercepts to solve strict and inclusive inequalities, including translated squares and irrational boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly suggested quadratic formula to find exact intercepts, then interpret each parabola's sign and whether endpoints are included.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 explicitly requests graphical solutions and supplies the quadratic-formula cue for irrational intercepts.
questions.methodNote: Find intercepts, then select where the parabola lies above or below the x-axis; include intercepts for non-strict inequalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find irrational boundary values using the quadratic formula and interpret the sign graphically.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete the square as instructed and use its non-negativity to justify a strictly positive lower bound for every real x.

questions.mappingNote: This proof is directly specified by the question, and the teacher solution confirms the completed-square argument.
questions.methodNote: The embedded instruction requires completing the square; use the non-negativity of a real square.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square and use non-negativity to justify strict positivity for every real value.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a perfect square and justify why a non-positive square must be zero.

questions.mappingNote: The task is the repeated-root case of a quadratic inequality; the teacher solution confirms the sole solution.
questions.methodNote: Factorise as instructed and use non-negativity of a square, retaining the equality boundary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a perfect square and justify why a non-positive square must be zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the usual inequality procedure: recognise the interval endpoints as roots, then recover the constant using a root or the monic factorisation.

questions.mappingNote: The given interval is essential student-visible information, allowing the roots and constant coefficient to be recovered.
questions.methodNote: Use the relationship between intercepts and the interval where an upward-opening parabola is negative.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the roots from a solution interval and recover the constant term.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate algebraic intersections with graph features: rearrange line equations, solve the resulting quadratics, recover both coordinates, and sketch consistently, including repeated-root tangency.

questions.mappingNote: All eleven assigned parts pair a parabola with a line and directly assess line–curve intersections. Parts (e) and (g) have a repeated intersection; part (f) requires exact irrational roots. The printed exercise is 17G, despite the supplied page-level topic metadata identifying the later 17H heading.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the two expressions for y, rearranges and solves the quadratic, substitutes each x-value into an original equation, then sketches both graphs with their features and labelled intersections. Its part (a) contains a substitution typo: 3-(-2)=5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a line and parabola using their features and solve for intersections, including a repeated intersection and irrational coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Equate two parabola expressions, handle cancellation or factorisation, recover intersection coordinates, and coordinate both curves' vertices and intercepts in one sketch.

questions.mappingNote: All eleven parts assess this same procedure for pairs of parabolas. The closest catalogue intersection skill is intersection-line-curve, supplemented by parabola sketching and quadratic factorisation. Page 20 concerns the next exercise and is not needed for these tasks.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the two expressions for y, expands and factorises where needed, substitutes each x-value to obtain y, then sketches the functions and labels intersections and axial intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Equate two quadratic functions, solve for their intersections and sketch both parabolas using their features.

classification.difficultyReason: Finds a unique intersection algebraically using two distinct symbolic parameters.

questions.mappingNote: Applies the same intersection method to two translated parabolas with symbolic parameters. The closest supplied skill covers algebraic curve intersections.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the expressions for y, expands and rearranges, solves for x, and substitutes into an original equation to obtain y.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds a unique intersection algebraically using two distinct symbolic parameters.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct two distinct quadratic equations satisfying both point constraints, choosing suitable coefficients or transformations and checking that their intersections are the specified points.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 reverses the intersection task by requesting two parabola equations through specified points. The proposed equations are checked using the taught equating, factorising and substituting method.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the two expressions for y, rearranges and factorises, then substitutes each x-value to obtain the intersection coordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct two distinct quadratic equations satisfying two given intersection points.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise both the vertical-line possibility and the tangent, parameterise a non-vertical line through the specified point, and impose a repeated intersection to derive its slope symbolically.

questions.mappingNote: This is Section G question 5 above the Section H topic band. Its most advanced directly assessed method is determining a parameter using a zero discriminant.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 equates the two equations, solves the resulting equation and substitutes to obtain intersection coordinates. For the single-intersection parameter task, the matched teacher solution uses the repeated-root discriminant condition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derives a general tangent equation using a repeated-root condition and identifies the vertical line permitted by the unrestricted stem.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires proving existence and uniqueness of a common point for an entire parameterised family of parabolas.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the same equating-and-substitution method to two distinct members of the family, then verify the resulting point for every coefficient.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the two expressions for y, solves for x, then substitutes to obtain y.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires proving existence and uniqueness of a common point for an entire parameterised family of parabolas.

classification.difficultyReason: Find symbolic intersections and distinguish two, one or no real intersections from the parameter values.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the same equate-and-substitute method to two parameterised parabolas. The intersection skill is the closest supplied taxonomy match.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 equates the two expressions for y, solves the resulting quadratic and substitutes each x-value to find y.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find symbolic intersections and distinguish two, one or no real intersections from the parameter values.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the labelled vertex and endpoint to determine model coefficients, infer seven interior cable positions from equal spacing, and sum the corresponding heights, optionally using symmetry.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 uses the same model and seven-cable structure with endpoint (16,12) and vertex (0,4); finding the equation from graphical features is the main assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 19 introduces the suspension-bridge model. Page 20 Example 1 obtains k from the turning point, substitutes an endpoint to find c, and sums evenly spaced cable lengths using symmetry.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine coefficients from the vertex and an endpoint, then use symmetry to sum seven cable lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret roots and the vertex physically, then solve the height-threshold equation and select the interval where the downward trajectory exceeds six metres.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 repeats the fountain structure with y=2x(4-x) and threshold 6 m. The quadratic inequality in part (c) is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 Example 2 and its solution on page 21 use the horizontal intercepts for distance, their midpoint for maximum height, and factorisation of the height-equality equation followed by graphical interpretation for an exceedance interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret intercepts and the vertex, then find and interpret the interval above a specified height.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect roots and vertex to the physical flight, discard negative time, and convert the interval above the initial height into a duration.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 applies these taught methods to a ball launched above ground level. Interpreting the quadratic model covers the whole question, with graph sketching and a quadratic inequality as supporting skills.
questions.methodNote: The projectile introduction and Example 2 use roots to interpret the flight, their midpoint to locate the turning point, and a height-equality equation with graphical interpretation to find a height-exceedance interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch and interpret a projectile model, including flight time, an interval above the initial height and maximum height.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch and interpret both height models, translate the twice-height comparison into an equation, and retain launch time as a valid solution alongside the later time.

questions.mappingNote: Page 19 introduces 17H Applications of quadratics; page 20 introduces projectile motion and a quadratic-height example. Question 4 on page 22 precedes the new 17I band and matches Section H question 4 in the teacher answers, so it belongs to 17H rather than 17I.
questions.methodNote: Use the projectile-height model, find ground-level intercepts by factorising, locate each vertex halfway between the intercepts, and substitute to find maximum height. Equate the two height expressions for the requested comparison.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare two projectile models using intercepts, vertices and an equation relating their heights.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest part reverses the usual height-to-duration problem: use symmetry about the previously found maximum to place the one-second interval, then evaluate its endpoint height. Earlier parts supply the vertex and graph but do not explicitly direct this connection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 continues 17H Exercises, confirmed by the heading on source page 21. Its height, flight-time, maximum and interval questions apply the projectile-model method; part (e) requires an exact quadratic solution.
questions.methodNote: Applications of quadratics introduces projectile motion. Example 2 and its solution use intercepts, the midpoint of the intercepts for the turning point, and intersections with a horizontal height line to determine a duration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interprets a projectile model, constructs its graph and determines an unknown height from a prescribed duration.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the perimeter into a relation between the sides, substitute into the area formula, and find the quadratic maximum using the taught midpoint-of-intercepts method.

questions.mappingNote: Page 22 demonstrates the same four-sided fixed-perimeter rectangle problem. Page 23 reinforces substitution into the area function and the midpoint-of-intercepts method.
questions.methodNote: Express one side using the perimeter constraint, form the quadratic area function, and find its maximum halfway between its intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the taught fixed-perimeter rectangle optimisation method.

classification.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic area model from a three-sided fencing constraint and use its intercepts to locate the maximum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17I.2 has the same three-sided river-paddock structure as Example 1, with 360 metres of fencing instead of 120 metres. The directly assessed skill is solving the resulting optimisation problem without calculus.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 establishes a quadratic area model using a length constraint and locates the maximum halfway between its intercepts. Page 23 Example 1 applies this method to a paddock with a river boundary, using 2x+y equal to the fencing length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form a quadratic area model from a three-sided fencing constraint and use its intercepts to locate the maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the vertex coordinates as the rectangle's dimensions, substitute the supplied linear relation into its area, and maximise the resulting quadratic using the demonstrated method.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly adapts Example 2, replacing y=4-2x with y=8-2x. Quadratic optimisation is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the linear constraint into A=xy, factor the area quadratic, and find the maximum halfway between its intercepts, as demonstrated in Example 2 on pages 23–24.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an area quadratic from a coordinate constraint and locate its maximum using the midpoint of its intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the shared fence once to construct the fencing constraint, distinguish one paddock's area from the total, and then apply the familiar quadratic maximisation procedure.

questions.mappingNote: This question adapts the fencing example to two identical paddocks. The internal shared fence changes the constraint to 4x+3y=120, and the requested objective is the area of one paddock.
questions.methodNote: Express one dimension using the fencing constraint, substitute into A=xy, factorise the area quadratic and find its maximum halfway between the intercepts, as demonstrated in the introductory optimisation problem and Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count the shared fence once, form a quadratic area model and locate its maximum using the midpoint of its intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Part (c) extends the preceding numerical minimisations to a parameter: complete the square in x, interpret the remaining expression as the minimum, and equate it to 18 while retaining both signs of a.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for a quadratic minimum. Parts a and b apply the completing-the-square method directly; part c additionally equates the resulting minimum to 18 and retains both parameter values.
questions.methodNote: Page 24 Example 3 explicitly teaches completing the square and using non-negativity of the squared term to establish a minimum. Pages 22–23 introduce quadratic optimisation through constraints and turning points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete the square to determine minima, then use a prescribed minimum to determine a parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a linear constraint into the objective expression and complete the square to establish its minimum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17I.6 directly adapts Example 3's constrained algebraic minimisation, with coefficient 4 in place of 2. Solving optimisation is the closest catalogue skill; completing the square supplies the taught method.
questions.methodNote: Page 24 Example 3 substitutes a rearranged linear constraint into a quadratic objective, completes the square, and uses the non-negativity of the squared term to establish the minimum and equality case.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute a linear constraint into the objective expression and complete the square to establish its minimum.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied similar-triangles hint to identify corresponding sides and express the remaining base as 4−x, then turn that relation into a quadratic area function and maximise it.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 adds the supplied similar-triangles hint to the taught area-optimisation method. Optimisation is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Define the constraint, substitute into A=xy, and locate the maximum of the downward-opening quadratic halfway between its intercepts, as demonstrated in the rectangle examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use similar triangles to form an area quadratic, then find and interpret its maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Minimise the supplied quadratic separation by completing the square.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 belongs to Section I, confirmed by the individually matching teacher answer. Completing the square applies the supplied minimisation method directly; no calculus is required.
questions.methodNote: Pages 22–23 model a quadratic objective and interpret its turning point. Page 24 Example 3 completes the square to establish a minimum; Example 4 defines vertical separation by subtracting the lower ordinate from the upper ordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Minimise the supplied quadratic separation by completing the square.

classification.difficultyReason: Minimises a quadratic separation and generalises the result to a parameter, requiring interpretation when the curves intersect.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 belongs to quadratic optimisation, confirmed by the topic span and the teacher's Section I question 9. Both parts minimise a quadratic difference; part b additionally needs a distinction between signed difference and geometric separation.
questions.methodNote: Pages 22–24 model an objective function from a constraint and find its quadratic turning point. Page 24 Example 3 explicitly teaches completing the square; Example 4 defines vertical separation as the difference of function heights.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Minimises a quadratic separation and generalises the result to a parameter, requiring interpretation when the curves intersect.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires similar triangles to establish the constraint and a quadratic model to find the largest area.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 adds a similar-triangles constraint to the taught quadratic-area optimisation method. The topic and matching teacher Section I establish exercise 17I despite the inventory’s part3-17h metadata.
questions.methodNote: Express the area using the constraint, then locate the maximum of the downward-opening quadratic halfway between its intercepts, as in the introductory optimisation demonstration and Examples 1 and 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires similar triangles to establish the constraint and a quadratic model to find the largest area.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a linear demand model, form a quadratic profit function and interpret its maximum with monetary rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 applies this same intercept-midpoint method to profit after deriving a linear relationship from two price-demand pairs. The Section I teacher answer independently confirms the demand equation, profit function and price.
questions.methodNote: The optimisation introduction and Examples 1 and 2 form an objective function using a constraint, then locate the maximum halfway between the quadratic's intercepts.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a linear demand model, form a quadratic profit function and interpret its maximum with monetary rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a linear yield model from two observations, form a quadratic total yield and interpret its maximum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 belongs to Quadratic optimisation, exercise 17I. Its linear yield constraint produces a quadratic objective whose maximum determines the required planting count.
questions.methodNote: Define variables, express the constraint, form a quadratic objective and locate its maximum halfway between its intercepts, as demonstrated in the rectangle and paddock examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a linear yield model from two observations, form a quadratic total yield and interpret its maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand a parameterised sum of squares and use the position of its minimum to determine the number of terms.

questions.mappingNote: Question 13 belongs to 17I Quadratic optimisation, whose source band begins on page 22. It asks for a parameter from the location of a quadratic minimum; solve-optimisation is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Expand the objective into a quadratic and locate its minimum algebraically, following the quadratic optimisation teaching. The matched teacher solution uses the vertex formula after summing the coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand a parameterised sum of squares and use the position of its minimum to determine the number of terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a wire-allocation variable, convert the two allocated lengths into a square side and circle radius, and combine their areas into one quadratic. This requires coordinating two different perimeter-to-area relationships before applying the taught minimisation method.

questions.mappingNote: Question 14 belongs to section 17I, Quadratic optimisation, introduced on page 22. Its shared-length constraint and area objective directly assess quadratic optimisation.
questions.methodNote: Define the constraint, substitute into the area expression, and find the minimum of the resulting upward-opening quadratic. Page 24 also demonstrates completing the square for minimisation; the matched teacher solution uses the vertex formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires modelling two areas under a shared perimeter constraint and finding an exact quadratic minimum.
